Great reed warbler (Acrocephalus arundinaceus) eggs are incubated by the female for a period of approximately two weeks, and the age at birth is defined by the moment of hatching. Under controlled incubation conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the incubation period lasts exactly 14 days [ab = 14 days], a duration that aligns closely with values reported for other large-bodied acrocephaline warblers. Upon emerging from the egg, each neonate is remarkably small, with a measured wet weight at birth of just 2 grams [Wwb = 2 grams]. This minimal starting mass reflects the altricial developmental strategy of the species, wherein virtually all somatic growth and thermoregulatory capacity must be acquired post-hatching through intensive biparental provisioning. The newly hatched nestlings are entirely dependent on their parents for warmth and food, a phase that imposes substantial energetic demands on the attending adults during the first week after emergence.

As the altricial nestlings develop, their body mass increases rapidly under the combined influence of frequent feeding visits and brooding by both parents. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults of Acrocephalus arundinaceus has been documented at 25.7 grams [Wwi = 25.7 grams], although the AnAge database provides a slightly higher value of 30 grams [Wwi = 30 grams], possibly reflecting geographic variation in adult body size across the species' Palearctic range. This ultimate mass is achieved following the completion of the post-fledging growth period, during which juveniles refine their foraging skills. In terms of longevity, the maximum lifespan recorded for this species, as estimated from ring-recovery data under the active metabolic conditions typical of the breeding season at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], is approximately 10.1 years [am = approximately 10.1 years], a relatively extended lifespan for a passerine of its size and migratory habit.

Important developmental milestones occur in a precise sequence under the warm thermal conditions characteristic of the summer breeding period, when ambient body temperatures of an active adult average 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The time since birth at fledging, marking the age at which young first achieve sustained flight and leave the nest, is 13 days [tx = 13 days] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid nest departure is typical of certain marsh-nesting warblers, where predation risk in reed beds can be substantial, favoring a short nestling phase. Gonadal maturation initiates remarkably early in this species, with the onset of puberty occurring at 39 days after hatching [tp = 39 days after hatching] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a timing that reflects the selective pressure to reproduce within a single brief breeding season.

The reproductive schedule of the Great reed warbler is tightly constrained by the duration of the temperate breeding season. Females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a low annual fecundity that is partly offset by a moderate clutch size — a common life-history trade-off in long-distance migratory passerines, where the energetic demands of biannual trans-Saharan migration constrain the number of breeding attempts per season. Each clutch contains between 3 and 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 6 eggs per clutch], with a mean of approximately 4.5 eggs — a value that positions the Great reed warbler near the upper end of the clutch-size spectrum among European Acrocephalus species, reflecting the relatively stable food supply of productive reed-bed habitats. The maximum reproductive rate, achieved under optimal food availability and at the peak of the breeding season when ambient temperatures approach 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], corresponds to an annual output of approximately 4 to 5 eggs per year. This modest annual reproductive effort is a conservative life-history strategy, prioritizing adult survival in a migratory bird that faces significant energetic and predatory costs during its trans-Saharan journeys.

The timing of first reproduction is a key parameter shaping the species' population dynamics. The time since birth at first brood, defined as the interval from hatching to the laying of a female's first clutch, has been recorded at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This one-year delay means that individuals hatched in one summer do not typically breed until the following year, a pattern that aligns with the need to complete a full annual cycle of migration, overwintering in sub-Saharan Africa, and returning to European breeding grounds before attempting to nest. The reproductive timing is further modulated by local environmental conditions; in years with abundant reed aphid populations, some females may initiate their single annual clutch earlier in the season, thereby potentially improving fledgling survival by synchronizing hatch with peak prey availability for their growing young. Obligate single-brooding in this species thus reflects an evolutionary compromise between the benefits of multiple nesting attempts and the severe time constraints imposed by a long-distance migratory schedule, where arrival on the breeding grounds in late April leaves only a narrow window for nest-building, incubation, and chick-rearing before the southward journey recommences in August.
